item.title: How Israels war on Lebanons water has become existential
One Parts Bin, Three Wars: Beijing built a valve. We built a wall.
item.description:
Welcome to The Iron Triangle, the Cipher Brief column serving Procurement Officers tasked with buying the future, Investors funding the next generation of defense technology, and the Policy Wonks analyzing its impact on the global order.

In the industrial parks of Guangdong, the hardest part of the drone war is the visitor schedule. Ukrainian drone makers who travel to their Chinese component suppliers describe hosts who choreograph visits so that Ukrainian and Russian buyers never share a building. Separate doors. Service corridors. Empty conference rooms. Oleksandr Yakovenko, founder of TAF Industries, one of Ukraine's largest drone producers, told the Financial Times that his suppliers "try to make it so we will not be in the same factory at the same time." By the paper's account, the car carrying the Russians pulls out and the car carrying the Ukrainians pulls in.

That is not a supplier. That is a referee. And this month the referee is rewriting the rules.

The Valve

On October 19, Beijing published Announcement No. 49, revising dual-use export controls on 13 categories of drone components and technology, effective November 18. It reaches heavy multirotor motors and speed controllers, long-range autopilots, inertial navigation, datalinks, and engines. Read the signature block before the parts list: the notice was issued by the Ministry of Commerce, the General Administration of Customs, and the Equipment Development Department of the Central Military Commission. The military's equipment office co-signed Beijing's drone controls in 2023 too. This was never trade policy.

The design matters more than the scope. Announcement 49 bans nothing. It requires licenses, and licensing allows treatment to differ by exporter, destination, and end user. A ban is a wall. A license is a valve, and Beijing keeps its hand on it.

The second date resolved itself the day this column went to the editor, and the way it resolved is the point. China's suspension of its sweeping October 2025 rare earth controls, the ones that reach any foreign product containing as little as 0.1 percent Chinese-origin rare earth by value, was due to lapse on November 10. For six weeks the diplomacy said January while the legal notice said November. On November 9, with one day to spare, Beijing extended the pause to January 10. Two months. Nothing closed, and every magnet buyer in the West spent the autumn planning for a license queue anyway. A valve does not have to turn to work. It only has to be seen in someone's hand.

Three Wars, One Parts Bin

Start with what these parts do. By the Financial Times's count, drones account for up to three quarters of recent losses in Ukraine. The parts bin is where the killing power comes from.

Moscow. China's share of Russia's imports of the goods the G7 flags as battlefield priorities rose from 54.3 percent in 2022 to 84.6 percent in 2025. Russia does not have a supply chain. It has a supplier.

Kyiv. Ukraine has worked to get out. At the start of 2024, nearly 90 percent of its imported drone components came directly from China. In the first eight months of 2026, the figure was 28 percent. The number flatters. Some of the parts arriving through Poland and the Czech Republic were most likely made in China too, and Yakovenko told the Associated Press that switching entirely to Western parts could raise costs by as much as 60 percent and cut production by about the same. Andrii Taganskyi, whose company Odd Systems builds drone cameras, summed up the rest: "Without this 5%, there is no camera."

Then there is the detail that should keep Brussels up at night. In July, the EU let Kyiv spend part of a €5.9 billion drone tranche of its defense loan on Chinese components, because Europe cannot make enough of them. That loan is money Europe borrowed on the capital markets, to be repaid if Russia ever pays reparations. So European debt, backed by a Russian IOU, buys Chinese parts for Ukrainian drones, from the same supplier base arming Russia. Nobody planned that, but everybody signed it.

Taipei, by way of Washington. If you think the valve only turns for Europe's war, ask Skydio. In October 2024, Beijing sanctioned America's largest drone maker after Washington approved defense assistance for Taiwan. Chinese authorities visited Skydio's suppliers, including a TDK battery subsidiary in Dongguan, and told them to stop. Skydio rationed batteries to one per drone. Its only customer in Taiwan, the company pointed out, was the National Fire Agency. Its customer in Ukraine had ordered thousands of drones. A decision about Taiwan became battery rationing at the company supplying Ukraine. One parts bin, three wars.

The Wall We Built

Washington's answer has been prohibitions. On January 1, the DFARS magnet restriction expands to bar contractors from delivering neodymium-iron-boron and samarium-cobalt magnets if any step in the chain, from mining through refining, melting, and finished production, takes place in a covered country. Since September 3, Proclamation 11055 has imposed Section 232 duties of 10 to 100 percent on imported drones and components.

Each measure is defensible. Together they make a wall with very little stacked behind it. On June 30, the Army opened its first domestic small-drone motor line at Tobyhanna Army Depot, 1,500 motors a day. Adamas Intelligence, which tracks the magnet trade, reports that the magnets inside those motors are still roughly 90 percent Chinese-made. The Pentagon knows it. In May, the Defense Logistics Agency placed $25.8 million in sole-source orders with two U.S.-based magnet makers and paid $2 million to qualify a third. Set $25.8 million beside a program buying drones by the hundred thousand. The magnet rule has exceptions, including one for commercial off-the-shelf items, and they will be used, because the alternative is an idle motor line. A wall you have to keep waiving is not a wall. This is not a scandal. It is a feature of buying the airframe and hoping the bill of materials sorts itself out.

The tariff has its own irony. Taiwan, the democracy building a "non-red" drone supply chain as national policy, is slated to pay a reduced but real 15 percent combined rate on its drones. We are taxing the exit.

For the Procurement Officer

The Drone Dominance Program wants more than 200,000 one-way attack drones. Call it 800,000 motors. Chinese brushless motors have sold for $12 to $25 against $100 to $225 for American equivalents. Those were smaller motors at last year's prices, so treat the result as an order of magnitude: the premium to buy every one of those motors outside China lands somewhere around $60 to $170 million. The program is worth $1.1 billion. Independence for the most exposed component costs less than a rounding error on Golden Dome. You are not short of money. You are short of a contract that buys components instead of airframes.

The Investment Thesis

The bottleneck premium is moving down the bill of materials. Airframe makers are plentiful; hundreds applied to fly the Gauntlet. Magnet makers, motor winders, and camera-sensor houses that can document a clean chain back to the mine are not. On January 1, the documentation becomes the product. Price accordingly.

The Policy Wonk's Warning

Beijing has built the only arms-control regime of the drone age that is actually effective. No treaty, no verification, no Senate ratification. Just a licensing desk that can decide, case by case, whose drones fly in Ukraine. It has already used that desk to punish a Taiwan decision. Assume it will do so again when the Strait gets tense, and that the first sign will be paperwork, not ships.

My Take.

We do not need a wall. We need our own valve, and building one takes three moves.

First, pool demand. Washington's Drone Dominance money and Europe's Ukraine loan should buy components, not just finished drones, on multi-year offtake contracts that a magnet plant can take to a bank.

Second, write one list. Taiwan's ITRI is already the only overseas certifier in the U.S.-led Green UAS program. On October 27, at a forum in Taipei co-hosted by Taiwan's foreign ministry, John Hemmings of the Henry Jackson Society proposed that Taiwan and Europe agree on a red-free standard, certify suppliers, and stand up a drone supply chain office to write the testing rules. Fold Ukraine in, add the United States, and make it one certified-supplier list across the alliance.

Third, make the list worth something. Certified allied components should enter at zero duty. The proclamation already carves out zero-rate lanes for approved onshoring plans. Extend that logic to allies who are onshoring for all of us.

That is how a parts bin becomes an alliance.

The Risk.

The valve leaks. Ukrainian firms keep finding ways around Chinese restrictions through intermediaries, and Chinese factories have little appetite for losing a customer that size. Announcement 49 also aims high: standard five- and seven-inch FPVs fall below its motor thresholds, while heavy-lift and long-range systems take the hit. A fair reader could say Beijing is managing a market, not picking a winner. My answer is the last six weeks. Beijing closed nothing, and the West planned around it anyway. A regime that can be precise is more dangerous than one that is blunt, because it can squeeze one end user without disturbing anyone else's quarterly numbers.

Conclusion

Somewhere in Shenzhen this week, a sales manager is timing the cars in the parking lot so that two warring delegations never meet. America has already had its visit. In 2024 the men who came to the factory were Chinese officials, and the customer they cut off was ours. If Beijing can already decide which side's drones fly over Ukraine, what makes us so confident it will not decide whose fly over the Strait?

item.title: Iran Is Poking The Bear
item.description:
Tehran has been playing a dangerous game of chicken with the U.S. administration for months. With the just concluded midterms now in hand, they risk making a dangerous miscalculation just when it matters most. This is unlikely to end well.

With the continuation of strikes this week against international shipping transiting the Strait of Hormuz, while simultaneously engaging in renewed negotiations, Tehran is poking the bear with one hand while feeding it with the other. This is a dangerous strategy; they could lose a hand… or worse.

The Iranian leadership is clearly trying to have it both ways. Equal parts emboldened and wary, with a hefty dose of economic reality rapidly bearing down upon them.

Tehran is and always has been a keen observer of American politics. This time, however, they appear to be overconfident, and potentially risk acting on a tragic misreading of the situation. This two-pronged strategy - continued taunting, both verbal and military, while offering to negotiate, sort of – appears to indicate they perceive a deep new vulnerability in their opponent given the historic drubbing the administration received in the midterms. That is possible, and the administration will certainly face harsh scrutiny over its handling of the war. But it is also possible that they are seeing a President Trump who is merely stunned and, if such a thing is possible… humbled, if only for the moment. But this humility is unlikely to last. The President retains primary control over U.S. foreign and military policy, and there are already reports of plans for massive new strikes if negotiations again fail, or the President becomes frustrated with Tehran’s usual stalling and stubbornness.

The President is already looking for a fall-guy within his administration for a failed, unpopular war, and the devastating impact on the midterms; with the odds-on favorite(s) being Secretary of Defense Hegseth and/or senior military leaders. He is almost certain to look for one outside his administration as well, with Iran the certain candidate for their unwillingness to accede to the President’s attempts at diplomacy pre-election. He has proven that he is nothing if not vengeful. At the same time, the President wants a deal and appears ready for one. Unless, that is, Tehran insists on rubbing his face in a less than optimal resolution. This risks a reaction that would serve no one.

Tehran’s hubris is legend. As is that of President Trump. When these meet head-to-head – hubris to hubris – the result is at best uncertain, and potentially disastrous.

In the end, the most likely conclusion remains a negotiated settlement. Iran has several advantages, including geography, proven resilience and staying power. And their just-concluded conclave with Russia is a new, ominous development that bodes ill. On the other hand, the U.S. administration may finally have an effective strategy in its naval/economic blockade. But this will take time, and it may no longer have the political runway to see it through.

Tehran should declare victory and allow the U.S. President to go home. Face-saving measures are essential for both sides to avoid the additional death and destruction that is sure to follow military escalation, by either side.

But this will not be the final bell. Tehran will be left to its own devices to face the enormous challenges of a shattered economy, a degraded environment, and a restive population.

This is not over by a long shot.

I am reposting portions of a previous post given their continued relevance

Iran Is “Counting Coup” On The United States!

“Iran is playing a very dangerous game. In the face of the awesome military power of the United States, in between desultory negotiating sessions, they continue to touch the enemy by launching attacks against U.S. and allied Gulf facilities. Recently, they have reached farther afield, striking U.S. assets in an Egyptian port. This would seem to be inexplicable behavior, given the U.S.’s obvious desire for a deal, inviting as it has strong retaliatory strikes against Iran’s increasingly beleaguered military, and potentially civilian, infrastructure. Most recently, we are seeing reports of possible Iranian cyberattacks on the water supplies of U.S. cities; such activities are certain to continue and likely to escalate, plausibly deniable and effective in sowing fear as they are. The question is why?”

“It may be simple hubris. It may be a misread of the desperation of their opponent. Or simply overconfidence in the strength of their position. It most certainly is part and parcel of a purposeful negotiating strategy, a reminder to all involved that Iranian forces can reach out and touch you whenever they wish.

Regardless, they are walking a fine line, and they have placed this conflict squarely in the crosshairs of unintended consequences.

As they so often do, they risk overreaching. Should one of these missile or drone strikes make it through, whether by luck or skill, and inflict truly significant casualties on U.S. personnel, either in a land-based facility or on a naval vessel for example, this could surge American support for a massive response, possibly including – however unlikely – ground troops, radically altering and escalating the course of this conflict.”

“The Iranian leadership’s actions, however, are likely aimed not only at the United States but may be the result of continued factional maneuvering in Tehran, as groups jockey for advantage for what comes next. Now that it appears likely the regime will survive, they are no doubt looking ahead to where they will land in a new regime. As both factions and individuals.”

As I wrote in ‘Is Iran Controlling the Gulf Conflict?’: “I would posit that the newly ascended Supreme Leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, may in fact be a phantom leader. Alive in some fashion, perhaps largely incapacitated, but not actually in charge. And even if able to coherently express his views, in no way nearly as powerful or influential as his father. The seemingly reckless actions of the regime in courting U.S. retaliation may in actuality reflect a lack of a coherent decision-making process as opposed to a unified one. I think it is quite possible that competing factions within the regime are using Mojtaba as an avatar while they maneuver for decisive advantage.”

On 15 May, I laid out in “Ground Hog Day”, a recommended way forward for the U.S. that I think largely still applies. It is a measure of how fruitless continued military action is that these remain relevant today:

“Make a deal with Iran. One that they will accept. This will require painful concessions and is certain to include provisions that many will find objectionable, including significant sanctions relief. And it will leave the Iranian regime in place and in control of Iran. For now.”

“As much as I would prefer to see regime change in Iran, I believe a deal may be the only realistic way out of the Groundhog Day-like doom loop in which we find ourselves. Simply put, the administration squandered the initial opportunity presented by a unique confluence of events by its lack of strategic planning and a fundamental misunderstanding of Iran and the Iranian regime.”

“As a result, we are going to have to step back and take a longer view. I pity the people of Iran, at least in the near term. They are certain to suffer the brunt of the regime’s immediate ire. That is a hard truth.”

“This is not, however, the end of the story. Iran’s internal weaknesses still matter–and may shape what comes next more than battlefield successes. I am cautiously, very cautiously optimistic that even barring regime change, Iran’s leadership will be forced to change direction.”

“The issues facing Iran prior to the War were serious, in fact existential – a collapsing economy, hyper-inflation, severe water shortages, lack of electricity, and growing widespread popular anger and unrest – and are ongoing and only getting worse. Whatever the Iranian leadership looks like, it will have to address these issues. And it is not clear that they will be capable of doing this without outside help. This is where the U.S. and hopefully our Western allies come in: sanctions relief, and extensive economic and other assistance in exchange for real changes in policy and a pullback on objectionable activities and programs. The potential for this may, and I say may, have increased with the removal of Ali Khamenei from the Supreme Leader’s seat. But it will depend on whether his son and successor, Mojtaba, is less rigidly ideological than his father. We will see if he is willing to put the Iranian people ahead of the regime.”

It is becoming more obvious by the day that the U.S. needs to come to a negotiated settlement with Iran. And the terms of this settlement are certain to be painful and unsatisfactory from the perspective of the West. But continuing tit-for-tat airstrikes simply prolongs the pain and risks horrific unintended consequences without solving the problem, as well as providing the regime with a distraction from its appalling management of Iran’s economy, natural resources, and foreign policy.

An enraged and restive Iranian population awaits. Let the regime face, without fear or favor, the fruits of its mismanagement, leaving it to confront what it fears most: the streets. This is likely where genuine regime change will occur.

item.description: Germany’s Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution, the country’s domestic intelligence agency, confirmed to iStories and Deutsche Welle that it is questioning Russians at Berlin’s airport.

item.title: Europe taps national security advisers to represent the continent in Russia-Ukraine peace talks
item.description: National security advisers from the European Union, Germany, France, the United Kingdom, Italy, and Poland will represent Europe in upcoming talks on ending the Russia-Ukraine war, Bloomberg reported.

item.title: Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement
item.description:
Turkey and Qatar announced on Friday that they signed a mutual defence agreement, which they said was aimed at adopting a "unified position" in the face of an external attack.

The announcement came after Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan met Qatari Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani in Istanbul.

Erdogan had said the agreement would further strengthen ties between the regional allies, according to his office.

Qatar's ruler travelled to Istanbul after attending the United Nations COP31 climate summit in southern Turkey.

item.title: UN rights chief demands Houthis return body of Yemeni staff member
item.description:
GENEVA, Nov 13 (Reuters) - The UN's human rights chief on Friday demanded the return of the body of a Yemeni staff member of his office who died of unknown causes weeks ago after being held in Houthi custody for more than two years.

Mohammad el Shami's family learned of his death on October 30, more than a month after it occurred, but they have received no explanation of the cause or circumstances. El Shami had been held by the Houthi group since June ​6, 2024.

item.title: Turkey, Qatar sign mutual defence agreement, pledge unified stance against attack
item.description:
ISTANBUL, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Turkey and Qatar signed a mutual defence agreement on Friday aimed at strengthening collective defence and promoting regional security, and pledged a unified stance against any external armed attack targeting either country, according to a joint statement issued after talks between their leaders.

The two sides agreed to consult on threats to their security, as well as regional and global security issues and defence policies, and to expand cooperation through joint military exercises, defence-industry cooperation and personnel training exchanges.

item.title: Judges close part of ICC Afghanistan investigations that could look at US troops
item.description: THE HAGUE, Nov 13 (Reuters) - Judges at the International Criminal Court have issued a decision to formally close part of the prosecutor's investigations into Afghanistan that previously looked at alleged crimes by US troops and to focusonly on actions of the Taliban since 2021, court documents show.

item.title: Syria rolls back new visa restrictions for US citizens after backlash: What to know
item.description: A number of Syrians on social media criticized the change, saying it would harm efforts to draw tourists to the post-war country.

item.title: Oil returns to surplus as Gulf exports rebound through wartime disruptions
item.description: Oil supplies overtook consumption by almost 2 million barrels per day in October, according to data from the International Energy Agency released Friday.
